sections.title: Jacketed Filter Vessel Engineering
sections.tabSummary: What the flange, seal, and BOV design actually deliver
body: Every part of this vessel's design targets one of two problems: losing temperature control during filtration, or losing product to the equipment itself.

The jacket runs the full height down to the filter plate, not just around the reaction zone, which is what keeps temperature control consistent through both steps. The bottom outlet valve is built with zero dead space specifically to stop material collecting below the filter media, and it's removable for cleaning with a 15 mm bore for easy run-off. The seal between vessel and lid, an FEP-encapsulated O-ring with a PTFE collar on the DN100 flange, is what keeps the whole system leak-tight under those conditions.

sections.tabSummary: What actually changes when you make the switch
body: The comparison that actually matters for Mini isn't against Flex or Pilot, it's against the round-bottom flask and heating mantle it's meant to replace.

A flask on a mantle gives you heat, roughly. It doesn't give you a defined temperature range down to -70°C or up to 230°C, precise dosing, or the kind of reproducibility that shows up when a method needs to transfer to someone else's bench, let alone scale up later. Mini closes that gap at the exact volume most early discovery chemistry actually runs at, and because the vessel geometry matches the rest of the Reactor-Ready range, the eventual move to a larger system isn't a redesign.

longForm.heroHook: Trade the round-bottom flask for a jacketed reactor. Same small scale, precise temperature control.
heroParagraphs: A round-bottom flask on a heating mantle works, until precise temperature control actually matters. Mini gives you that control without asking you to scale up.

It runs the same -70°C to +230°C range as Radleys' full-size Reactor-Ready systems, in a footprint built for 50 mL to 500 mL vessels. The vessel geometry matches the rest of the range too, so when a project does need to scale up later, the transition is confident, not a redesign.

Vessels swap fast, dosing runs precisely, and because the working volume stays small, so does your solvent and material use. Process development starts earlier, with the safety and reproducibility a real jacketed system brings that a heating mantle never could.
